recommended_title: Missingness-Aware Latent Models for Budgeted Embedding Benchmark Prediction
central_question: How accurately can a historical-only, missingness-aware latent-model procedure predict an unseen embedding model’s recorded but unqueried benchmark scores at small query budgets, and how does this change under name-proxy-family-disjoint evaluation and destroyed historical cross-task alignment?
central_thesis: On the evaluated English MTEB panels, the frozen latent-model procedure has lower aggregate prediction error than the evaluated random-acquisition low-rank and greedy-coverage ridge pipelines, including on never-queryable audit targets, but the advantage is not uniform across held-out splits and does not isolate the contribution of mixtures or value-adaptive acquisition.
narrative_rationale: The strongest evidence is the completed final evaluation and its row/checkpoint records, not the search ordering or unverified internal diagnostics: these support direct error-versus-budget comparisons, common-target audits, an adverse family-disjoint split, and a historical-column permutation control. One shared question covers two split conditions on a single pinned embedding benchmark source; these are not independent datasets. The paper is an empirical method-integration study with explicit limits, not a new-architecture claim, a universal benchmark-compression result, or a campaign report. Final qualification is independently reported as completed/qualified by final.qualification.status and final.qualification.outcome; that administrative outcome is not evidence of universal validity, superiority, or mechanistic attribution.

Select the frozen evaluated latent-model family, with the two split conditions as evidence blocks under one thesis.

method_groups.name: Historical-only missingness-aware latent prediction and transfer selection
method_groups.include_reason: The frozen studied procedure fits observed-data low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance, considers a small latent-mixture extension, conditions on revealed scores, and uses historical fixed-target validation with a Gaussian fallback. Present it as one validation-selected procedure, not separately measured component methods.

method_groups.name: Random acquisition with masked low-rank prediction
method_groups.include_reason: A genuinely executed comparison with explicit per-row/checkpoint records and final MAE; it changes both fitting and acquisition relative to the proposed procedure, so it is not an isolated acquisition ablation.

method_groups.name: Greedy correlation-coverage acquisition with ridge prediction
method_groups.include_reason: The stronger evaluated comparator uses overlap-shrunk historical correlations for coverage and ridge prediction. Retain its adverse-to-proposed family-disjoint split; it is a whole-pipeline comparator, not a matched predictor control.

method_groups.name: Historical per-benchmark mean
method_groups.include_reason: Provides a simple historical-only reference. Fixed-audit errors are available in observation records; primary remaining-target errors use the proposed policy’s residual target sets and must be described accordingly.

method_groups.name: Historical-column permutation, queried-score average, and reset replay
method_groups.include_reason: Permutation preserves recorded masks and column marginals while disrupting cross-task alignment; the queried-score-average control tests a deliberately weak score-copying alternative; replay checks deterministic reset behavior. These are distinct controls, not independent methods or evidence that any one proposed component is necessary. Keep the queried-score average and replay detail in the supplement.

figure_plan: Figure 1, early on page 1 or 2: one conceptual overview of a masked historical matrix, historical-only latent fitting and model choice, a query/condition loop, and prediction/scoring on unqueried recorded cells, with a visually distinct never-queryable audit boundary.

Figure 2, primary results: two-panel fixed-audit MAE versus query budget, one panel per split condition, comparing the frozen procedure, greedy ridge, and random low-rank; show the three split-seed values and their descriptive means.

Figure 3, dependence diagnostic: two-panel original-versus-column-permuted history comparison on the same fixed audit targets, one panel per split condition, for the same three pipelines; retain individual split-seed points.

Main tables, not extra figures: a four-method aggregate remaining-target/common-audit comparison and a six-row split-by-seed proposed-versus-ridge comparison that makes the adverse split visible. Complete checkpoint/control tables belong after references.
